title: With Due Respect (Vol. 7) -- Ch. 3: Justice and Love on Valentine's Day
keywords: Justice and Love on Valentine's Day
Second National Congress of the Clergy
primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7) -- CJP's February 14, 2010 Inquirer column, a Valentine's reflection drawn from his address to the Second National Congress of the Clergy (5,500 strong), relating 'the juristic duty of dispensing justice to the priestly work of spreading God's love'

His unforgettable visit to the Muntinlupa national penitentiary -- undertaken despite security warnings after a Mass on Matthew 25 -- and the inmates' warm welcome, talent show, and his message of hope behind bars

An inmate's piercing question -- if all commandments reduce to loving God and neighbor, and a confessor forgives with a rosary, why must a judge punish? -- and CJP's struggle to reconcile his life of dispensing justice with the Lord's commandment of love

His answer from Matthew 25 (the Lord himself 'making choices' as both judge and lover) and the parable of the judge who fines his own repentant daughter, then pays the fine himself -- God being 'both the Lord of justice and the Lord of love,' as His priests and magistrates must be
sub_topics: The occasion: 'awed and mesmerized,' CJP addressed the Second National Congress of the Clergy -- 'before 5,500 cardinals, archbishops, bishops, and priests' -- asked to relate 'the juristic duty of dispensing justice to the priestly work of spreading God's love,' and wrote this Valentine's (and Chinese New Year) summary

Visit the prisons: after serving the Court 'over 11 years,' he recalls visiting the Muntinlupa penitentiary against Security's advice (the inmates 'could become unruly; after all, [he] sent many of them to jail') -- going only after a Mass on Matthew 25, telling himself 'better to risk the ire of the inmates than to incur the ire of the Lord'

The welcome: surprised by the penitentiary's sheer size (hectares of fruit trees around the 'concrete behemoth' for maximum-security inmates), he was met by some 500 inmates with applause, a band playing 'Mabuhay' and the anthem, and a talent show of comedy, folk dances and singers mimicking Sinatra and Celine Dion

Hope in prison: he spoke 'boldly of hope' -- that iron bars may restrict and bring ridicule, but the inmates should 'not hate the world and lose their faith,' for 'almost everyone is in some kind of prison' (the rich 'by their greed,' others by 'incurable illnesses,' the mentally ill 'by their minds'), and those behind bars at least have the hope of release, unlike those condemned by greed or illness 'to pain... all their lives'

The inmate's question: as he left, an inmate asked why, if all commandments reduce to 'Love God and love your fellow beings,' and a confessor merely 'asked me to pray the rosary and forgave me,' the judge could not do likewise -- 'Isn't love inconsistent with the punishment you imposed on me?'

The struggle: the question kept CJP thinking -- 'Isn't our Lord a God of love first and foremost? Why then should I... take pride in my work of imposing penalties? Is my career of dispensing justice contradictory to the Lord's commandment of love?'

The answer from Matthew 25: he found it in the same Gospel, where 'the Lord was judging his people' -- condemning to 'eternal punishment' those who did not feed, clothe or visit the needy, and granting 'eternal life' to those who did -- so the Lord too 'was making choices because he was the Lord of justice just as He was also the Lord of love'

The young lady's tale: he closes with a parable -- a judge fines a repentant speeding driver P500, then 'removed his robe... and paid the fine' himself, because the driver was his daughter; he 'had to let justice be done though the heavens may fall,' yet love moved him to pay -- just as 'our Father in heaven' rendered justice on sinners yet 'sent His only Son to redeem them,' so 'must His priests' and 'His magistrates'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's February 14, 2010 Inquirer column, is a Valentine's reflection from his address to the Second National Congress of the Clergy -- 'before 5,500 cardinals, archbishops, bishops, and priests' -- relating 'the juristic duty of dispensing justice to the priestly work of spreading God's love.' He recalls visiting the Muntinlupa penitentiary against Security's warnings (he had 'sent many of them to jail'), going only after a Mass on Matthew 25 and reasoning it 'better to risk the ire of the inmates than to incur the ire of the Lord.' Some 500 inmates welcomed him with applause, a band and a talent show; he spoke 'boldly of hope,' noting that 'almost everyone is in some kind of prison' -- the rich 'by their greed,' others by 'incurable illnesses,' the mentally ill 'by their minds' -- and that the incarcerated, who may be freed or pardoned, can be freer than these. As he left, an inmate asked why, if all commandments reduce to loving God and neighbor and a confessor forgives with a rosary, a judge must punish -- 'Isn't love inconsistent with the punishment?' The question made CJP wonder whether 'dispensing justice [is] contradictory to the Lord's commandment of love,' and he found his answer back in Matthew 25, where the Lord himself, judging the nations, condemns some to 'eternal punishment' and grants others 'eternal life' -- proof that 'the Lord too was making choices because he was the Lord of justice just as He was also the Lord of love.' He closes with a parable: a judge fines his repentant speeding daughter P500, then 'removed his robe... and paid the fine' himself -- justice done 'though the heavens may fall,' yet love bearing the cost -- just as 'our Father in heaven' punished sin yet 'sent His only Son to redeem,' so 'must His priests' and 'His magistrates.'
